intro: Every day you describe people and things: a new teacher, your little brother, a pair of lost headphones, how you feel before a game. In Spanish, describing starts with two verbs that both mean to be, ser and estar, and with adjectives that change their endings to match what they describe.

This unit shows you how to choose between ser and estar: ser for who someone is, where they are from, what they are like, the time and events; estar for where someone is and how they feel or are doing right now. Then you will learn to make adjectives agree in gender and number, place them in a sentence, and compare people with más… que, menos… que, mejor, peor, mayor and menor.

By the end you will be able to describe a family member, a friend or a famous person in a clear paragraph, explain every verb you chose, and fix the most common mistakes English speakers make, like la casa blanco or la fiesta está en mi casa.
bigQuestion: How do Spanish speakers describe who someone is, how they are right now, and how they compare to others?

words.d: to be — identity, origin, traits, time, dates and events: soy, eres, es, somos, sois, son
to be — location, feelings and conditions: estoy, estás, está, estamos, estáis, están
to be from, or to be made of — Soy de Chicago; La mesa es de madera
Where is it? — location always uses estar
happy, pleased — a feeling, so it uses estar: Estoy contenta
tired — a condition: Estamos cansados
with ser: clever; with estar: ready
with ser: boring; with estar: bored
adjective — a describing word that matches its noun in gender and number
intelligent — one form for both genders; plural inteligentes
more… than — Ana es más alta que Luis
older — Mi hermana es mayor que yo; menor means younger

test.q: Which form completes the sentence? Yo ___ de Honduras.
test.why: Origin uses ser, and yo takes soy.

test.q: Which sentence says We are at the museum?
test.why: Location of people uses estar; nosotros takes estamos.

test.q: Which sentence says It's two o'clock?
test.why: Time uses ser; two o'clock is plural: son las dos.

test.q: What does Mi primo está aburrido mean?
test.why: Estar aburrido describes a feeling: bored.

choices: La fiesta está en el parque.
La fiesta es en el parque.
La fiesta estás en el parque.
La fiesta son en el parque.

test.q: Which sentence says My mom is a doctor?
test.why: Jobs use ser without un or una, and doctora matches mamá.

test.q: Choose the adjective: Las ventanas están ___.
test.why: Ventanas is feminine plural, so abiertas.
Ojos is masculine plural; café adds -s: cafés.

test.q: Which phrase says a great idea?
test.why: Grande becomes gran before a singular noun and means great; idea is feminine: una.

test.q: Which sentence says Luis is less tall than Ana?
choices: Luis es menos alta que Ana.
Luis es menos alto de Ana.
Luis es menos alto que Ana.
Luis está menos alto que Ana.
test.why: Menos + adjective + que; alto agrees with Luis.

choices: Mis abuelos son más mayores que mis padres.
Mis abuelos son mayor que mis padres.
Mis abuelos están mayores que mis padres.
Mis abuelos son mayores que mis padres.
test.why: Mayor needs no más and becomes mayores in the plural.

test.q: Which question asks what someone is like?
test.why: ¿Cómo eres? uses ser and asks about traits.

test.q: Choose the adjective: Mi hermana es muy ___.
test.why: Paciente ends in -e, so it has one form for both genders; hermana is singular.

test.q: What does La sopa está rica mean?
choices: The soup is rich in money.
The soup is from a rich family.
test.why: Estar rico describes how food tastes.

test.q: Which pair fits? Mi amigo ___ simpático, pero hoy ___ triste.
test.why: A personality trait takes ser; a feeling today takes estar.

write.prompt: Escribe un párrafo sobre una persona importante en tu vida. Write a paragraph in Spanish (6–8 sentences) that says who the person is and where they are from, describes their looks and personality, tells how they are or where they are today, and includes one comparison with más… que, menos… que, mayor or menor.
tips: Use ser for identity, origin and traits; use estar for location and how the person feels today.
Check every adjective against its noun: -o or -a, singular or plural.
Put most adjectives after the noun, and use tener for hair and eyes.
Use que in comparisons, and never write más mejor.
Read it aloud, then read again looking only at endings and accents.

title: Ser, Estar and Describing People

chapters.title: Two Verbs for To Be
chapters.bigQuestion: How can one English verb, to be, need two Spanish verbs, and how do you choose the right one?

story.title: Two Cousins at the Same Party
story.kicker: Mateo is always calm. Daniela is calm only today, and Spanish can hear the difference.
paragraphs: Mateo and Daniela are cousins, and both live in Little Village in Chicago. At their grandmother's birthday party, their aunt introduces them to a new neighbor. She points to Mateo and says, "Mateo es tranquilo" (Mateo is a calm person). Everyone nods. Mateo never raises his voice, even when his little brothers spill juice on his homework.

Then the aunt points to Daniela, who is usually loud, funny and full of energy. Today Daniela is sitting quietly in the corner with a plate of tamales. The aunt says, "Daniela está tranquila hoy" (Daniela is calm today). Daniela laughs, because she knows the word está means this is how she is right now, not who she always is.

The neighbor, a student learning Spanish, asks a question in English: "Why did you say es for Mateo and está for Daniela? Aren't they both just is?" The aunt smiles. "In English, yes. In Spanish we have two verbs: ser and estar. Ser tells what someone is like as a person. Estar tells how someone is at this moment, or where someone is."

Later the grandmother opens her gifts and says, "¡Estoy muy contenta!" (I am very happy!). Then she adds, "Soy de Michoacán" (I am from Michoacán). The neighbor listens closely and starts to notice a pattern. Feelings and places use estar. Where you come from and what you are like use ser.

By the end of the party the neighbor tries it herself: "Soy estudiante y estoy cansada" (I am a student and I am tired). Daniela gives her a thumbs up. One sentence, two verbs, two different kinds of being.
story.think: Think of one thing about you that is always true and one thing that is true only today. Which one would use ser and which would use estar?

lessons.title: All the Forms of Ser
lessons.mainIdea: Ser is irregular: soy, eres, es, somos, sois, son, and you must memorize these forms.
reading: Picture your first day in a new Spanish class. The teacher says, "Yo *soy* la profesora Ruiz" (I am Professor Ruiz). A student answers, "Yo soy Carlos." Both sentences use the verb *ser* (to be), and both tell who someone is. Ser is one of the most common verbs in Spanish, so you will hear it every day.

Ser is irregular, which means its forms do not follow a normal pattern. You cannot just drop an ending and add a new one. Here are all six present-tense forms: yo soy (I am), tú eres (you are, friendly), él, ella or usted es (he, she is, or you are, formal), nosotros somos (we are), vosotros sois (you all are, used in Spain), ellos, ellas or ustedes son (they are, or you all are).

Say them in order out loud: soy, eres, es, somos, sois, son. Notice that eres and es look alike but are different. Eres goes only with tú: "Tú eres mi amigo" (You are my friend). Es goes with one other person or with usted: "Ella es mi amiga" (She is my friend).

A common mistake is to say "yo es" because English uses is so often. In Spanish each subject has its own form. Yo always takes soy. Another mistake is to forget the verb completely: "Yo estudiante." Spanish needs the verb, so say "Yo soy estudiante."

words.d: to be — for identity, origin, traits, time and dates; irregular: soy, eres, es, somos, sois, son
I am — the yo form of ser: Soy estudiante (I am a student)
you are — the tú form of ser: Eres simpático (You are nice)

look.title: Introductions in the Hallway
look.text:
Ana: Hola, yo soy Ana. ¿Tú eres nuevo? (Hi, I'm Ana. Are you new?)
Luis: Sí, soy Luis. Mi hermana y yo somos de Texas. (Yes, I'm Luis. My sister and I are from Texas.)
Ana: ¡Qué bien! Mis padres son de Puerto Rico. (Great! My parents are from Puerto Rico.)
look.prompt: Find every form of ser in the dialogue and name its subject. Then introduce yourself with two sentences using soy.

check.q: Which form of ser completes the sentence? Nosotros ___ de Chicago.
check.why: Nosotros (we) takes somos: Nosotros somos de Chicago.

check.q: Which sentence is correct?
check.why: Tú always takes eres; es is for él, ella and usted.

check.q: What does Ellos son estudiantes mean?
check.why: Son is the ellos form of ser, so the sentence means they are students.

lessons.title: All the Forms of Estar
lessons.mainIdea: Estar is also irregular: estoy, estás, está, estamos, estáis, están, with accents on most forms.
reading: Imagine texting your cousin after school. She writes, "¿Dónde *estás*?" (Where are you?). You answer, "Estoy en casa" (I am at home). Both messages use the verb *estar* (to be), the verb Spanish uses for where you are and how you are right now.

Here are the six present-tense forms of estar: yo estoy (I am), tú estás (you are), él, ella or usted está (he, she is, or you are, formal), nosotros estamos (we are), vosotros estáis (you all are, Spain), ellos, ellas or ustedes están (they are, or you all are). Estoy ends in -oy, just like soy, voy and doy.

Watch the accent marks. Estás, está, estáis and están all have a written accent, and it changes where you put the stress: es-TÁ, not ES-ta. Without the accent, esta means this (esta casa, this house). So "Ella está aquí" (She is here) needs the accent, but "esta mesa" (this table) does not.

English speakers often drop the accent because English has none. In Spanish a missing accent can create a different word, so write it every time. Estamos is the one form besides estoy that has no written accent, because its stress falls naturally on -ta-.

words.d: to be — for location, feelings and conditions; forms: estoy, estás, está, estamos, estáis, están
I am — the yo form of estar: Estoy en clase (I am in class)
you are — the tú form of estar, with an accent on the a: ¿Cómo estás? (How are you?)

look.title: A Quick Text Thread
look.text:
Prima: ¿Dónde estás? (Where are you?)
Tú: Estoy en la biblioteca con Ana. Estamos cansadas. (I'm at the library with Ana. We're tired.)
Prima: Mis padres están en el mercado. (My parents are at the market.)
look.prompt: List every form of estar in the texts and write its subject. Then write a text telling a friend where you are right now.

check.q: Which form completes the sentence? Mis amigos ___ en el parque.
check.why: Mis amigos is ellos, which takes están, written with an accent on the a.

check.q: Which sentence is spelled correctly?
check.why: The tú form is estás, with a written accent; está goes with él, ella or usted.

check.q: Which form of estar has NO written accent?
check.why: Estoy and estamos have no written accent; estás, está, estáis and están do.

lessons.title: Why Spanish Has Two
lessons.mainIdea: Ser tells what something is; estar tells where it is or how it is right now.
reading: Look at two sentences about the same cup of hot chocolate. "El chocolate es delicioso" means chocolate is delicious as a general fact. "El chocolate está caliente" means the chocolate is hot right now. English uses is for both. Spanish uses two verbs because it separates what something is from the state it is in.

A simple way to think about it: ser answers the question What is it? or What is it like? Estar answers Where is it? or How is it right now? This is a starting point, not a perfect rule, but it works for most sentences you will say in middle school.

Both verbs come from Latin. Ser comes mostly from the Latin verb esse (to be). Estar comes from stare, which meant to stand. That history still shows: estar describes where something stands and the condition it stands in at the moment.

Many learners try to choose based on whether something is permanent. That idea helps sometimes, but it fails with some examples. A person who has died "está muerto" (is dead), which is permanent, yet it uses estar because it is a condition. Learn the uses one by one instead of relying only on permanent versus temporary.

words.d: hot (temperature) — often with estar: La sopa está caliente (The soup is hot)
delicious — Los tacos son deliciosos (Tacos are delicious, in general)
now — a clue that you are describing a present state: Ahora estoy bien

look.title: Same Soup, Two Sentences
look.text:
Abuela: La sopa de mi mamá es muy buena. (My mom's soup is very good, always.)
Nieto: ¡Y hoy la sopa está muy caliente! (And today the soup is very hot!)
Abuela: Espera un minuto. Ahora está perfecta. (Wait a minute. Now it's just right.)
look.prompt: Why does the grandmother use es in the first line and está in the last line? Write one sentence of each kind about your favorite food.

check.q: Which question does estar usually answer?
choices: Where is it, or how is it right now?
check.why: Estar is for location and present states; material, time and origin use ser.

check.q: What does El café está frío mean?
choices: Coffee is a cold drink in general.
The coffee is from a cold place.
The coffee is cold right now.
check.why: Está describes the coffee's condition at this moment.

check.q: Why does La abuela está muerta use estar even though death is permanent?
choices: Being dead is treated as a condition, which takes estar.
Estar is always used for permanent facts.
It is a mistake; ser is correct.
check.why: Spanish treats muerto as a resulting condition, so it takes estar; permanent versus temporary is only a rough guide.

lessons.title: Identity and Profession
lessons.mainIdea: Use ser to say who someone is, what they are, and what job they have.
reading: At a family reunion someone asks, "¿Quién es él?" (Who is he?). You answer, "Es mi tío Roberto. Es enfermero" (He's my uncle Roberto. He's a nurse). Both answers use ser, because they tell who he is and what he does. Identity, relationships and jobs all take ser.

Notice something new: Spanish says "Es enfermero," not "Es un enfermero." When you name someone's job, religion or nationality after ser without any description, you leave out un or una. "Mi mamá es profesora" (My mom is a teacher). English speakers often add un because English needs a.

If you add a description, the un comes back: "Es un enfermero excelente" (He is an excellent nurse). The description makes it about this particular person, so the article returns. You will see this pattern in school documents all the time.

Relationships also use ser: "Ella es mi hermana" (She is my sister), "Somos amigos" (We are friends). A frequent mistake is using estar here, as in "Está mi hermana." That sounds like she is present in a place, not who she is to you.

words.d: the nurse (male); la enfermera is a female nurse — Es enfermero (He is a nurse)
the teacher (female); el profesor for a male teacher
Who is it? / Who is he or she? — answered with ser

look.title: Family Photo
look.text: Look at a family photo. "Esta es mi mamá. Es doctora. Este es mi papá. Es cocinero en un restaurante en Pilsen. Y este soy yo. Soy estudiante." (This is my mom. She is a doctor. This is my dad. He is a cook at a restaurant in Pilsen. And this is me. I am a student.)
look.prompt: Describe three people in your life using ser: who they are to you and what they do. Leave out un or una before the jobs.

check.q: Which sentence correctly says My aunt is a lawyer?
check.why: Jobs use ser, and Spanish drops una before an undescribed job after ser.

check.q: How do you ask Who is she?
check.why: Identity questions use ser: ¿Quién es?

check.q: When does un come back before a job?
choices: When you add a description, like un doctor muy bueno
check.why: An adjective describing the person brings back the article: Es un doctor muy bueno.

lessons.title: Origin and Nationality
lessons.mainIdea: Use ser de to say where someone or something is from, and ser with nationality words.
reading: A new classmate says, "Soy de Guatemala" (I am from Guatemala). Another says, "Mi familia es de Chicago, pero mis abuelos son de Puerto Rico." Where people come from is part of who they are, so origin always takes ser plus de (from).

Nationality words also use ser: "Ella es mexicana" (She is Mexican), "Ellos son colombianos" (They are Colombian). In Spanish, nationality words are not capitalized. English writes Mexican with a capital M, but Spanish writes mexicana with a small m.

Things have origins too. "El café es de Colombia" (The coffee is from Colombia). "Estas tortillas son de una tortillería en Little Village" (These tortillas are from a tortilla shop in Little Village). Ser de can also mean made of: "La mesa es de madera" (The table is made of wood).

Compare origin with location. "Soy de Chicago" tells where you are from. "Estoy en Chicago" tells where you are now. A student from Chicago on vacation in Miami says, "Soy de Chicago, pero estoy en Miami."

words.d: to be from, or to be made of — Soy de Illinois; La silla es de metal
Mexican — nationality words are lowercase in Spanish; mexicana for a female
wood — La mesa es de madera (The table is made of wood)

look.title: Where Are You From?
look.text:
Profesor: ¿De dónde eres? (Where are you from?)
Sofía: Soy de Chicago, pero mi mamá es de Ecuador. (I'm from Chicago, but my mom is from Ecuador.)
Profesor: ¿Y dónde está tu mamá ahora? (And where is your mom now?)
Sofía: Está en Quito con mi abuela. (She's in Quito with my grandmother.)
look.prompt: Why does Sofía use es for her mom's origin and está for where her mom is now? Answer the question ¿De dónde eres? in Spanish.

check.q: Which sentence says Marta is from Peru?
check.why: Origin uses ser de: es de Perú.

check.q: Which is written correctly in Spanish?
check.why: Nationality uses ser, is lowercase, and agrees in number: cubanos.

check.q: What does La camisa es de algodón mean?
choices: The shirt is in the cotton.
The shirt is made of cotton.
check.why: Ser de can tell what something is made of.

lessons.title: Traits and Characteristics
lessons.mainIdea: Use ser with adjectives that describe what someone or something is like in general.
reading: Think back to Mateo from the story: "Mateo es tranquilo." That sentence describes his personality, the kind of person he is. Traits like personality, looks, size and color usually take ser: "Mi hermano es *alto*" (My brother is tall), "Mi perro es *simpático*" (My dog is friendly).

Walk through a description: Mi abuela es baja (short), es muy inteligente y es generosa. Each adjective tells what she is like, not how she feels today, so each uses ser. The adjectives also end in -a because abuela is feminine.
Things have traits too. "La casa es grande" (The house is big). "El libro es interesante" (The book is interesting). "La nieve es blanca" (Snow is white). These describe the thing as it normally is.

Learners sometimes use estar for looks: "Mi hermano está alto." A native speaker might hear that as He's looking tall today, or He's gotten tall. Use ser for normal traits unless you really mean a change.

words.d: tall — Es alto (He is tall); alta for a female, altos and altas for plurals
nice, friendly — describes personality: Mi prima es simpática
generous — Mi abuela es generosa (My grandmother is generous)

look.title: Describe a Friend
look.text: Mi amiga Lucía es alta y delgada. Es muy divertida y un poco tímida. Sus ojos son cafés. (My friend Lucía is tall and slim. She is very fun and a little shy. Her eyes are brown.) Every verb here is a form of ser, because each sentence says what Lucía is like.
look.prompt: Write three sentences about a friend's traits using ser. Make each adjective match your friend: -o or -a.

check.q: Which sentence describes a personality trait?
check.why: Divertido (fun) describes what he is like, so it uses ser.

check.q: Choose the correct form: Las casas ___ grandes.
check.why: Size as a trait uses ser, and las casas (they) takes son.

check.q: What might Mi primo está alto suggest to a native speaker?
choices: He is a tall person by nature.
He has gotten tall or looks tall now.
He is standing on a table.
He is from a tall city.
check.why: Estar with a trait signals a change or impression, not the normal trait.

lessons.title: Time, Dates and Events
lessons.mainIdea: Use ser to tell time, give dates and days, and say where an event takes place.
reading: Your friend asks, "¿Qué hora es?" (What time is it?). You look at your phone: "Son las tres" (It's three o'clock). Telling time uses ser. For one o'clock use es: "Es la una." For every other hour use son, because the hours are plural: "Son las dos, son las diez."

Dates and days use ser too. "Hoy es lunes" (Today is Monday). "Mañana es el 16 de septiembre" (Tomorrow is September 16), Mexico's Independence Day. Notice that Spanish puts the day number before the month and does not capitalize days or months.

Here is a surprise: the location of an event uses ser, not estar. "La fiesta es en mi casa" (The party is at my house). "El concierto es en el parque" (The concert is in the park). An event takes place somewhere, and Spanish treats that as ser.

Compare two sentences. "La fiesta es en la escuela" (The party takes place at school). "Mis amigos están en la escuela" (My friends are at school). People and objects are located with estar; events happen with ser. Many English speakers use está for both, which is a very common error.

words.d: the hour, the time — ¿Qué hora es? (What time is it?)
the party — La fiesta es el sábado (The party is on Saturday)
the concert — an event, so its location uses ser: El concierto es en el parque

look.title: Clock Times (Examples)
look.cite: Example clock times written in standard Spanish
look.prompt: Why does only one row start with Es instead of Son? How would you say it's 3:00?

check.q: How do you say It's one o'clock?
check.why: One o'clock is singular, so it takes es: Es la una.

check.q: Which sentence is correct for The concert is at the stadium?
choices: El concierto está en el estadio.
El concierto son en el estadio.
El concierto estar en el estadio.
El concierto es en el estadio.
check.why: The place where an event happens uses ser.

check.q: Which sentence correctly gives today's day?
check.why: Days use ser, and days of the week are lowercase in Spanish.

lessons.title: Location of People and Things
lessons.mainIdea: Use estar to say where a person or object is located.
reading: You can't find your backpack. Your mom says, "Tu mochila está en la cocina" (Your backpack is in the kitchen). Any time you say where a person or thing is, use estar. "Estoy en la escuela." "Chicago está en Illinois." "Mis llaves están en la mesa."

Even places that never move use estar for their location. "El lago Michigan está al este de Chicago" (Lake Michigan is east of Chicago). "Madrid está en España." The city is always there, yet Spanish still uses estar, because the sentence is about location.

Useful location words go after estar: *cerca de* (near), lejos de (far from), al lado de (next to), encima de (on top of), debajo de (under). "La biblioteca está cerca de mi casa" (The library is near my house).

The question word is dónde (where): "¿Dónde está el baño?" (Where is the bathroom?). A common mistake is "¿Dónde es el baño?" Remember: objects and people are located with estar, and only events use ser for place.

words.d: Where is it? — the location question, always with estar
near — La tienda está cerca de la escuela (The store is near the school)
far from — Puerto Rico está lejos de Chicago

look.title: Where Is Everything?
look.text: Picture your kitchen. El refrigerador está al lado de la estufa. La fruta está encima de la mesa. El gato está debajo de la silla. Mi hermano está en su cuarto. (The fridge is next to the stove. The fruit is on the table. The cat is under the chair. My brother is in his room.)
look.prompt: Describe where four things are in your classroom using estar and cerca de, al lado de, encima de or debajo de.

check.q: How do you ask Where is the library?
check.why: Location of a place takes estar, singular está with its accent.

check.q: Which sentence is correct?
check.why: Even a permanent place uses estar for its location.

check.q: What does Los libros están debajo de la cama mean?
choices: The books are on the bed.
The books are next to the bed.
The books are far from the bed.
The books are under the bed.
check.why: Debajo de means under.

lessons.title: Feelings and Moods
lessons.mainIdea: Use estar for emotions and moods: how someone feels right now.
reading: The grandmother in the story opens her gifts and says, "¡Estoy muy contenta!" (I'm very happy!). Feelings are states that change during the day, so they take estar. "Estoy *nervioso*" (I'm nervous) before a test. "Estoy tranquilo" after it ends.

Common feeling words with estar: contento (happy), triste (sad), enojado (angry), nervioso (nervous), preocupado (worried), aburrido (bored), emocionado (excited). Each changes to match the person: "Mi hermana está preocupada." "Mis amigos están emocionados."

The question is "¿Cómo estás?" (How are you?). You might answer "Estoy bien" (I'm well) or "Estoy un poco triste" (I'm a little sad). Asking "¿Cómo eres?" is a different question: it means What are you like? and you would answer with traits.

One word breaks the pattern: feliz (happy). Many speakers say "Soy feliz" for a happy life and "Estoy feliz" for right now, and both are correct. For a safe choice, use estar contento for a feeling today.

words.d: happy, pleased — a feeling, so it uses estar: Estoy contenta
nervous — Estoy nervioso antes del examen (I'm nervous before the test)
angry, mad — Mi papá está enojado (My dad is angry)
How are you? — asks about your feelings or health right now

look.title: Before and After the Test
look.text:
8:00 a.m. — Marco: Estoy muy nervioso. (I'm very nervous.)
9:00 a.m. — Marco: Estoy cansado, pero estoy contento. (I'm tired, but I'm happy.)
3:00 p.m. — Marco: ¡Estoy emocionado! Saqué una A. (I'm excited! I got an A.)
look.prompt: Why does Marco use estar every time? Write how you feel at three different times of your school day.

check.q: Which sentence says We are worried?
check.why: Feelings use estar; nosotros takes estamos and the adjective is plural.

check.q: What is the difference between ¿Cómo estás? and ¿Cómo eres?
choices: They mean exactly the same thing.
The first asks how you feel; the second asks what you are like.
The first is formal; the second is friendly.
The first asks your name; the second asks your age.
check.why: Estar asks about your state now; ser asks about your character.

check.q: Choose the correct form: Ana ___ triste hoy.
check.why: A feeling today takes estar, and Ana takes está with an accent.

lessons.title: Conditions and Health
lessons.mainIdea: Use estar for physical conditions: sick, tired, broken, open, clean, full.
reading: You wake up with a sore throat and text your teacher: "Estoy *enfermo*" (I'm sick). Health is a condition, so it takes estar. "Estoy cansada" (I'm tired). "Mi abuelo está mejor" (My grandfather is better).

Objects have conditions too. "La puerta está abierta" (The door is open). "La tienda está cerrada" (The store is closed). "Mi teléfono está roto" (My phone is broken). "El cuarto está limpio" (The room is clean). These describe the state things are in right now.

Watch how a condition can change while the object stays the same. "La ventana está abierta" in the morning, and later "La ventana está cerrada." The window did not become a different window; only its condition changed.

A mistake to avoid: "Soy enfermo" or "Soy cansado" for how you feel today. With ser, those can sound like a permanent description of who you are. For how you are today, use estar. Say "Estoy enferma" instead.

words.d: sick, ill — a condition: Estoy enfermo (I'm sick)
tired — Estamos cansados después del partido (We're tired after the game)
open — La tienda está abierta (The store is open); cerrado means closed

look.title: A Note to the Nurse
look.text: Picture the school nurse's office. A student says: "Estoy enfermo. Estoy cansado y la garganta está roja." (I'm sick. I'm tired and my throat is red.) The nurse answers: "La clínica está abierta hasta las tres. Descansa aquí." (The clinic is open until three. Rest here.)
look.prompt: Write three sentences with estar about conditions you see around you right now: something open or closed, clean or dirty, and how you feel.

check.q: Which sentence says The store is closed?
check.why: Open or closed is a condition, so estar; the adjective matches tienda (feminine).

check.q: What does Mi hermano está enfermo mean?
choices: My brother is a sick person by nature.
My brother is in the hospital building.
check.why: Estar plus enfermo describes a present health condition.

check.q: Why is Soy cansado a problem for I'm tired today?
choices: Tiredness now is a condition and needs estar.
Soy is the wrong person for yo.
Spanish has no word for tired.
check.why: Conditions right now take estar: Estoy cansado.

lessons.title: Aburrido and Listo
lessons.mainIdea: Some adjectives change meaning with ser or estar: es aburrido is boring, está aburrido is bored.
reading: Your friend yawns during a movie and says, "Estoy aburrido." He means I'm bored, a feeling right now. If he said, "Soy aburrido," he would mean I'm a boring person. Same adjective, different verb, very different message.

Aburrido works like this: ser aburrido means boring (a trait), estar aburrido means bored (a feeling). "La película es aburrida" (The movie is boring). "Los estudiantes están aburridos" (The students are bored).

Listo is another pair: ser listo means clever or smart, estar listo means ready. "Mi prima es muy lista" (My cousin is very clever). "¿Estás lista?" (Are you ready?). Before a trip your mom might shout, "¡Estamos listos!" (We're ready!).

These pairs make sense if you use the core idea. Ser gives the trait or identity. Estar gives the state right now. Being ready is a state; being clever is a trait. Once you see that, the meanings are easy to remember.

words.d: with ser: boring (La clase es aburrida); with estar: bored (Estoy aburrido)
with ser: clever, smart (Es lista); with estar: ready (Está lista)

look.title: Getting Out the Door
look.text:
Mamá: ¿Están listos? Vamos a llegar tarde. (Are you ready? We're going to be late.)
Hijo: ¡No! Estoy aburrido de esperar a mi hermana. (No! I'm bored of waiting for my sister.)
Hija: ¡Ya estoy lista! Y yo soy lista: tengo el mapa. (I'm ready now! And I'm clever: I have the map.)
look.prompt: Find each use of listo and aburrido. Which ones are traits and which are states? Write your own pair of sentences with listo.

check.q: What does La clase es aburrida mean?
check.why: Ser plus aburrido describes a trait: boring.

check.q: How do you ask a girl Are you ready?
check.why: Ready is estar listo; tú takes estás and a girl takes lista.

check.q: What does Mi hermano es muy listo mean?
check.why: Ser listo means clever or smart.

lessons.title: Rico, Malo and Verde
lessons.mainIdea: More pairs: ser rico is rich, estar rico is tasty; ser malo is bad, estar malo is sick; ser verde is green, estar verde is unripe.
reading: At a taquería in Pilsen, your uncle bites into a taco al pastor and says, "¡Está *rico*!" (It's delicious!). He is not calling the taco wealthy. With estar, rico describes how food tastes right now. With ser, "Es rico" usually means He is rich.
Malo follows the same idea. "Ese perro es malo" (That dog is bad, as in mean). "Mi abuela está mala" (My grandmother is sick) in many countries. The trait is bad; the state is unwell.

Colors can change too. "La manzana es verde" (The apple is green, a green apple). "El plátano está verde" (The banana is unripe, not ready to eat). The ser sentence names a color; the estar sentence describes its condition.

You do not need to memorize a long list. Ask yourself each time: am I describing what this is, or the state it is in right now? That question explains every pair in this lesson. Try it with any new adjective you meet.

words.d: with ser: rich (Es rico); with estar: tasty, delicious (La sopa está rica)
with ser: bad, mean (Es malo); with estar: sick or gone bad (Está malo)
green; with estar about fruit: unripe (El mango está verde)

look.title: At the Fruit Stand
look.text:
Vendedor: Los mangos son de México. Son muy dulces. (The mangos are from Mexico. They are very sweet.)
Cliente: Este mango está verde, ¿no? (This mango is unripe, right?)
Vendedor: Sí, pero este está perfecto. ¡Pruébalo! (Yes, but this one is perfect. Try it!)
Cliente: ¡Mmm, está riquísimo! (Mmm, it's delicious!)
look.prompt: Explain each es and está in the dialogue. Then say one food that está rico today and one thing that es verde.

check.q: What does El pozole está muy rico mean?
choices: The pozole is very rich in money.
The pozole is from a rich place.
check.why: Estar rico describes how food tastes.

check.q: What does El plátano está verde mean?
choices: The banana is green by nature.
The banana is from a green place.
check.why: Estar verde with fruit means not yet ripe.

check.q: Which sentence says That man is rich?
check.why: Wealth is a trait, so ser rico; hombre takes the masculine rico.

lessons.title: Common Errors and a Final Test
lessons.mainIdea: Check ser or estar by asking: is this identity, origin, trait, time or event, or is it location, feeling or condition?
reading: Here is a quick checklist to use while you write. Ser: description (traits), origin, occupation, characteristics, time, events, relationships, identity. Estar: location, feelings, conditions, results. Some teachers use short memory tricks for these lists, but the questions What is it? and How or where is it now? work just as well.

Error one: "La fiesta está en mi casa." Events take ser, so the correct form is "La fiesta es en mi casa." Error two: "Soy en la clase." Location of a person takes estar: "Estoy en la clase." Error three: "Estoy de Chicago." Origin takes ser: "Soy de Chicago."

Error four is the adjective ending. "Mi mamá está cansado" has the right verb but the wrong ending; it should be cansada, because mamá is feminine. Always check the verb first, then check that the adjective matches.

Now test yourself on a full sentence: "Mi primo Diego es de Texas, es muy simpático, pero hoy está enfermo y está en casa." Origin, trait, condition, location: ser, ser, estar, estar. When you can explain every verb in a sentence like that, you understand both verbs.

words.d: adjective — a word that describes a noun and matches it: cansado, cansada
mistake, error — Es un error común (It's a common mistake)

look.title: Fix the Paragraph
look.text: A student wrote: "Mi amiga Rosa está de Honduras. Ella está muy inteligente. Hoy es cansada y es en la biblioteca. La fiesta de Rosa está el sábado." (My friend Rosa is from Honduras. She is very intelligent. Today she is tired and she is at the library. Rosa's party is on Saturday.) Every verb is wrong.
look.prompt: Rewrite the paragraph with the correct verb in each sentence and name the rule for each fix.

check.q: Which sentence is correct?
choices: La reunión es en el gimnasio.
La reunión está en el gimnasio.
La reunión son en el gimnasio.
La reunión estás en el gimnasio.
check.why: A meeting is an event, and the place an event happens takes ser.

check.q: What is wrong with Mis hermanas están cansado?
check.why: Estar is right for tiredness, but the adjective must be feminine plural: cansadas.

check.q: Which pair of verbs fits? Mi tío ___ de Cuba y ahora ___ en Miami.
check.why: Origin takes ser (es de Cuba); present location takes estar (está en Miami).

review.q: Which is the yo form of ser?
review.why: Ser: soy, eres, es, somos, sois, son.

review.q: Which sentence says They are in the gym?
review.why: Location of people uses estar; ellos takes están, with an accent.

review.q: Which sentence says It's four o'clock?
review.why: Time uses ser; hours after one are plural: son las cuatro.
Estar listo means ready; ser listo means clever.

review.q: Which sentence correctly says My parents are Colombian?
review.why: Nationality takes ser, is lowercase, and agrees with the plural subject.

review.q: In the story, why does the aunt say Daniela está tranquila hoy?
choices: Daniela is calm only today, not usually.
Daniela is always a calm person.
Daniela is from a calm town.
Daniela is sitting in a calm place.
review.why: Estar describes a present state that is different from her usual personality.

choices: La boda está en la iglesia.
La boda es en la iglesia.
La boda estás en la iglesia.
La boda soy en la iglesia.
review.why: A wedding is an event, so its location uses ser.

review.q: What does La película es aburrida mean?
review.why: Ser aburrido describes a trait: boring.

chapters.title: Adjective Agreement and Description
chapters.bigQuestion: How do Spanish adjectives change to match the people and things they describe?

story.title: The Lost-Dog Poster
story.kicker: Canela is missing, and the poster has to describe her so clearly that anyone could spot her.
paragraphs: On a cold Saturday morning in Humboldt Park, eleven-year-old Gabriel opens the back door and finds the gate open. His dog Canela is gone. His grandmother, who reads Spanish better than English, says they need a poster in both languages, fast. Gabriel grabs markers and a big sheet of paper.

He writes the first line: "Perro perdido." His older sister Valeria stops him. "Canela is a girl. It should be perra perdida." Gabriel fixes it, then decides "Se busca perrita" (Looking for a little dog) sounds kinder. He starts describing her: "Es pequeña, café y muy simpática" (She is small, brown and very friendly).

Then he writes "Tiene orejas grande." Valeria points again. "Orejas is plural. Grandes, with an s." Gabriel groans, but he sees the pattern: every describing word has to match the word it describes, girl or boy, one or many. He rewrites it: "Tiene orejas grandes y una cola larga" (She has big ears and a long tail).

His grandmother adds one more line, comparing Canela to the neighbor's dog so people can picture her size: "Es más pequeña que un gato grande" (She is smaller than a big cat). They tape copies to lampposts all along the street and one inside the corner bakery.

That evening a neighbor knocks. She is holding Canela, muddy and happy. "I read your poster," she says in Spanish. "Pequeña, café, orejas grandes. I knew it was her right away." Good description, with every ending in the right place, brought Canela home.
story.think: If you had to describe your pet, your backpack or a friend so a stranger could find them, what three details would you choose, and how would each word change to match?

lessons.title: Gender Agreement: -o and -a
lessons.mainIdea: An adjective ending in -o changes to -a to match a feminine noun: el gato negro, la gata negra.
reading: Gabriel's first mistake on the poster was writing perdido for a girl dog. In Spanish, an adjetivo (adjective), a word that describes a noun, must agree with that noun. Agree means it matches the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and its number (one or more than one).

Most adjectives you learn first end in -o. That is the masculine form. To describe a feminine noun, change the -o to -a. Walk through it: el perro negro (the black dog), la perra negra (the black female dog). El libro nuevo (the new book), la mochila nueva (the new backpack).

Look at the noun, not the person talking. A boy describing his grandmother says, "Mi abuela es bonita" (My grandmother is pretty), with -a, because abuela is feminine. A girl describing her uncle says, "Mi tío es alto," with -o.

English speakers often forget agreement because English adjectives never change: a tall boy, a tall girl. In Spanish that habit produces mistakes like "la casa blanco." Train yourself to look back at the noun every time you write an adjective.

words.d: to agree, to match — adjectives concuerdan with nouns in gender and number
pretty, nice-looking — bonita for feminine nouns: una casa bonita
black — el gato negro, la gata negra
new — el libro nuevo, la mochila nueva

look.title: Switching the Ending
look.text: Start with the masculine: el chico alto → la chica alta. el carro rojo → la bicicleta roja. el perro pequeño → la perra pequeña. Step by step: find the noun, check if it is el or la, then give the adjective -o or -a to match.
look.prompt: Change each phrase to feminine: el maestro simpático, el hermano pequeño, el gato blanco. What stayed the same and what changed?

check.q: Which phrase is correct?
check.why: Camisa is feminine singular, so the adjective is roja.

check.q: Choose the adjective: Mi abuela es muy ___.
check.why: Abuela is feminine singular, so simpático changes to simpática.

check.q: What does agree mean for a Spanish adjective?
choices: It always goes before the noun.
It matches its noun in gender and number.
It matches the gender of the speaker.
check.why: Agreement means matching the noun described, not the speaker.

lessons.title: Number Agreement: Plurals
lessons.mainIdea: Plural nouns take plural adjectives: add -s after a vowel and -es after a consonant.
reading: Gabriel's second mistake was "orejas grande." Orejas (ears) is plural, so the adjective must be plural too: orejas grandes. Number agreement works the same way nouns make plurals. Plurals matter just as much as gender.

If the adjective ends in a vowel, add -s: alto → altos, bonita → bonitas, grande → grandes. If it ends in a consonant, add -es: azul → azules, fácil → fáciles, joven → jóvenes. Notice that joven gains an accent in the plural so the stress stays in the same place.

Now combine gender and number. There are four forms of an -o adjective: alto (masculine singular), alta (feminine singular), altos (masculine plural), altas (feminine plural). "Los chicos son altos. Las chicas son altas."

When a group mixes masculine and feminine nouns, use the masculine plural. "Mi hermano y mi hermana son simpáticos." Even one boy in a large group of girls makes the adjective masculine plural. This rule is the standard in Spanish grammar.

words.d: plural — more than one; adjectives add -s or -es: grandes, azules
blue — plural azules: los ojos azules (blue eyes)
young — plural jóvenes, which adds a written accent

look.title: Four Forms of One Adjective
look.text:
el perro alto (one male dog)
la perra alta (one female dog)
los perros altos (male dogs, or a mixed group)
las perras altas (female dogs)
An adjective ending in -e has only two forms: grande, grandes.
look.prompt: Write all four forms of pequeño with the nouns gato and gata. Then write the two forms of verde.

check.q: Which phrase is correct?
check.why: Azul ends in a consonant, so the plural adds -es; lápices is masculine.

check.q: Choose the adjective: Mi tío y mi tía son ___.
check.why: A mixed group takes the masculine plural.

check.q: What is the plural of el chico joven?
check.why: Joven adds -es and needs an accent: jóvenes; the noun also becomes plural.

lessons.title: Adjectives Ending in -e or a Consonant
lessons.mainIdea: Adjectives ending in -e or most consonants have one form for both genders: inteligente, fácil.
reading: Your teacher says, "Marco es *inteligente*. Ana es inteligente." The adjective did not change. Adjectives that end in -e have the same form for masculine and feminine. Only the number changes: los estudiantes inteligentes.

Most adjectives ending in a consonant work the same way. "El examen es *fácil*. La tarea es fácil" (The test is easy. The homework is easy). Other examples: difícil (hard), azul (blue), gris (gray), joven (young), popular (popular).
A common mistake is to invent a feminine form: "inteligenta" or "fácila." Those words do not exist. If the adjective does not end in -o, leave it alone for gender and change only for number.

There is one group that does change: nationality adjectives ending in a consonant, and a few ending in -or. Español becomes española; trabajador (hardworking) becomes trabajadora. "Mi mamá es muy trabajadora" (My mom is very hardworking).

words.d: intelligent, smart — same form for both genders: un chico inteligente, una chica inteligente
easy — plural fáciles; difícil means hard
hardworking — changes for feminine: trabajadora

look.title: Which Ones Change?
look.text: Sort these for a feminine noun like la maestra: alegre → alegre (no change). paciente → paciente. amable → amable. trabajador → trabajadora (changes). española → española (changes from español). divertido → divertida (changes).
look.prompt: Describe a woman you admire with three adjectives: one ending in -o, one ending in -e and one ending in -or. Show the correct forms.

check.q: Choose the adjective: La clase de matemáticas es ___.
check.why: Difícil ends in a consonant and does not change for gender; clase is singular.

check.q: Which sentence is correct?
check.why: Inteligente has one form for both genders; the plural adds -s.

check.q: Which adjective DOES change for a feminine noun?
check.why: Adjectives ending in -or, like trabajador, add -a: trabajadora.

lessons.title: Where Adjectives Go
lessons.mainIdea: Most describing adjectives go after the noun; number words and a few like buen and gran go before.
reading: English puts adjectives before the noun: a red car. Spanish usually puts them after: un carro *rojo*. "Una casa grande" (a big house). "Un perro simpático" (a friendly dog). Putting them first, as in "una roja casa," is a very common English-speaker error.

Some words go before the noun: numbers (dos gatos), mucho (mucha gente, a lot of people), poco, and the question words. These tell how many rather than what kind. "Tengo tres hermanos" (I have three siblings) and "Hay muchos libros" (There are many books) follow this order.

Bueno and malo can go before a masculine singular noun, and then they drop the -o: buen and mal. "Es un *buen* amigo" (He is a good friend). "Es un mal día" (It's a bad day). The feminine keeps its ending: "una buena amiga."

Grande becomes gran before any singular noun, and its meaning changes. "Una casa grande" is a big house. "Una gran casa" is a great house. "Es un gran presidente" means he is a great president, not a physically big one.

words.d: red — goes after the noun: un carro rojo, una manzana roja
good — short form of bueno before a masculine singular noun: un buen día
great — short form of grande before a singular noun: una gran idea

look.title: Flip the Order
look.text:
English: a white cat → Spanish: un gato blanco.
English: two new friends → Spanish: dos amigos nuevos.
English: a good book → Spanish: un buen libro (or un libro bueno).
English: a great woman → Spanish: una gran mujer.
look.prompt: Translate: a green backpack, three tall girls, a good teacher (male). Where did each adjective go?

check.q: Which phrase says a blue car?
check.why: Color adjectives go after the noun, and azul has no -a form.

check.q: Choose the correct phrase for a good friend (male):
check.why: Bueno shortens to buen before a masculine singular noun.

check.q: What does Es una gran ciudad mean?
check.why: Gran before a noun means great; grande after the noun means big.

lessons.title: Physical Description
lessons.mainIdea: Describe looks with ser plus an adjective and tener plus hair or eyes: Es alto. Tiene el pelo negro.
reading: The neighbor recognized Canela from three details. Describing people works the same way. Start with ser for build and height: "Es alto" (He is tall), "Es baja" (She is short), "Es delgado" (He is slim). Choose the ending that matches the person.

For hair and eyes, Spanish often uses *tener* (to have): "Tiene el pelo rizado" (He has curly hair), "Tiene los ojos verdes" (She has green eyes). Notice the adjective agrees with pelo or ojos, not with the person. A girl "tiene el pelo largo," with -o, because pelo is masculine.

Useful words: el pelo corto (short hair), largo (long), rizado (curly), lacio (straight), castaño (brown hair), rubio (blond). For eyes: los ojos cafés or marrones (brown eyes), azules, verdes. Café and marrón are both correct; different countries prefer different words.

Watch the false friend: largo means long, not large. "Tiene el pelo largo" is long hair. For large, use grande. English speakers mix these up often. "Una casa grande" is a big house, and "una calle larga" is a long street.

words.d: hair — Tiene el pelo corto (He or she has short hair)
eyes — Tiene los ojos verdes (He or she has green eyes)
long (not large) — el pelo largo, una falda larga
to have — used for hair and eyes: tengo, tienes, tiene

look.title: Spot the Person
look.text: Picture a crowded school hallway. "Busco a mi hermana. Es baja y delgada. Tiene el pelo largo y rizado y los ojos cafés. Lleva una mochila roja." (I'm looking for my sister. She is short and slim. She has long, curly hair and brown eyes. She's carrying a red backpack.)
look.prompt: Describe someone in the room so a classmate could find them: use ser for two traits and tener for hair and eyes.

check.q: Which sentence says She has long hair?
check.why: Tener is used for hair, and largo matches pelo (masculine); grande means big, not long.

check.q: Choose the adjective: Mi hermano tiene los ojos ___.
check.why: The adjective matches ojos, which is plural: azules.

check.q: What does Mi prima es baja y delgada mean?
choices: My cousin is tall and slim.
My cousin is short and slim.
My cousin is short and tired.
check.why: Baja means short in height and delgada means slim.

lessons.title: Personality
lessons.mainIdea: Personality traits use ser and agree with the person: Es generosa, son divertidos.
reading: Canela is "muy simpática" on the poster, and that tells people she is friendly, a personality trait. Traits of character use ser, because they describe what someone is like, not how they feel today.

Common personality words, in pairs of opposites: simpático / antipático (nice / unpleasant), trabajador / perezoso (hardworking / lazy), *divertido* / serio (fun / serious), tímido / extrovertido (shy / outgoing), generoso / egoísta (generous / selfish), *paciente* / impaciente.

Use small words to make descriptions sharper: muy (very), un poco (a little), bastante (quite), and no. "Mi papá es muy paciente, pero un poco serio" (My dad is very patient, but a little serious). "No es perezoso" (He is not lazy).

Egoísta ends in -a even for a man: "Él es egoísta." A few adjectives ending in -ista work this way; they have one form for both genders, like optimista and realista. "Mi hermano es optimista y mi hermana es realista" uses the same endings for both.

words.d: fun, funny — Mi tía es divertida (My aunt is fun)
lazy — Mi gato es perezoso; the opposite of trabajador
patient — same form for both genders: una maestra paciente
shy — Soy un poco tímida (I'm a little shy)

look.title: Opposite Twins
look.text: Lupe y Pablo son gemelos, pero son muy diferentes. Lupe es extrovertida y divertida. Pablo es tímido y serio. Lupe es un poco impaciente; Pablo es muy paciente. Pero los dos son muy generosos. (Lupe and Pablo are twins, but they are very different...)
look.prompt: Why does generosos end in -os at the end? Describe yourself with three personality words, using muy, un poco or no.

check.q: Choose the adjective: Mis hermanas son muy ___.
check.why: Hermanas is feminine plural, so trabajador becomes trabajadoras.

check.q: Which sentence is correct for He is selfish?
check.why: Egoísta keeps -a for both genders in the singular.

check.q: What does Mi abuelo es un poco serio mean?
choices: My grandfather is a little serious.
My grandfather is serious today only.
check.why: Un poco means a little, and ser describes his usual personality.

lessons.title: Describing a Family Member
lessons.mainIdea: A good description combines who the person is, looks, personality and a detail, each with the right verb and ending.
reading: Put the pieces together to describe someone you love. Start with identity and origin (ser): "Mi abuela se llama Rosa. Es de Jalisco, México." Add looks: "Es baja y tiene el pelo blanco y corto." Add personality: "Es muy cariñosa y un poco estricta."

Then add a detail that makes the person real, often with estar or another verb: "Ahora vive en Pilsen con mi familia. Hoy está contenta porque es su cumpleaños" (Now she lives in Pilsen with my family. Today she is happy because it's her birthday).

Check every adjective against the noun it describes. Abuela is feminine singular, so baja, cariñosa and estricta all end in -a. Pelo is masculine, so blanco and corto end in -o, even though the pelo belongs to a woman.

Heritage speakers often speak this naturally and still misspell endings or accents when writing. Read your description aloud, then read it again looking only at endings. That second check catches most mistakes.

words.d: grandmother — el abuelo is grandfather; los abuelos means grandparents
affectionate, loving — Mi abuela es muy cariñosa
strict — Mi papá es un poco estricto

look.title: A Paragraph About Tío Jorge
look.text: Mi tío Jorge es de Puerto Rico. Es alto y tiene los ojos cafés. Es muy divertido y generoso. Es cocinero y su comida es riquísima. Hoy está cansado porque trabaja mucho. (My uncle Jorge is from Puerto Rico. He is tall and has brown eyes. He is very fun and generous. He is a cook and his food is delicious. Today he is tired because he works a lot.)
look.prompt: Label each verb in the paragraph as identity, origin, looks, personality or condition. Then write five sentences about a family member.

check.q: Choose the adjectives: Mi mamá tiene el pelo ___ y es muy ___.
check.why: Negro matches pelo (masculine); cariñosa matches mamá (feminine).

check.q: Which sentence uses the right verb for Today my grandmother is happy?
check.why: A feeling today uses estar, and contenta matches abuela.

check.q: Why is the checking step of reading only the endings useful?
choices: It checks the meaning of each verb.
It replaces the need to check spelling.
It shows where to put accents on nouns.
It catches agreement mistakes that are easy to miss when speaking.
check.why: Agreement errors in endings are the most common written mistake, even for fluent speakers.

lessons.title: More Than and Less Than
lessons.mainIdea: To compare, use más + adjective + que or menos + adjective + que, with the adjective agreeing.
reading: Gabriel's grandmother wrote, "Es más pequeña que un gato grande" (She is smaller than a big cat). That is a comparison. The pattern is más + adjective + que for more than, and menos + adjective + que for less than.

Walk through it: Ana es alta. Ana es más alta que Luis (Ana is taller than Luis). Luis es menos alto que Ana (Luis is less tall than Ana). English often uses -er (taller), but Spanish always uses más; "altera" is not a word.

The adjective still agrees with the first person or thing: "Mi hermana es más alta que mi hermano." Alta matches hermana, the subject, not hermano. "Soy más alto que mi hermano" (I am taller than my brother) follows the same rule.

A frequent mistake is using de or como instead of que: "más alto de Luis" or "más alto como Luis." For comparing two people or things, use que. (Más de is used only before numbers, like más de diez, more than ten.)

words.d: more… than — Pedro es más alto que yo (Pedro is taller than I am)
less… than — El libro es menos interesante que la película
small, little — Mi perra es más pequeña que tu gato

look.title: Heights of Three Cousins (Example)
look.prompt: Write two true sentences: one with más alto/alta que and one with menos alto/alta que. How many centimeters taller is Ana than Marisol?

check.q: Which sentence says Sofía is taller than Pedro?
choices: Sofía es más alta que Pedro.
Sofía es más alto que Pedro.
Sofía es más alta de Pedro.
Sofía es alta más que Pedro.
check.why: Más + adjective + que; alta agrees with Sofía.

check.q: What does El español es menos difícil que el inglés mean?
choices: Spanish is more difficult than English.
Spanish is less difficult than English.
Spanish is as difficult as English.
Spanish is the most difficult language.
check.why: Menos… que means less… than.

check.q: Which word completes the comparison? Mi gato es más grande ___ tu perro.
check.why: Comparisons between two things use que.

lessons.title: Irregular Comparisons
lessons.mainIdea: Four common comparisons are irregular: mejor, peor, mayor and menor.
reading: You would not say more good in English; you say better. Spanish has the same kind of shortcut. Instead of más bueno, say *mejor* (better). Instead of más malo, say peor (worse). "Este taco es mejor que ese" (This taco is better than that one).
For age, Spanish uses *mayor* (older) and *menor* (younger). "Mi hermana es mayor que yo" (My sister is older than I am). "Mi primo es menor que mi hermano" (My cousin is younger than my brother).

These four words do not change for gender. "Mi hermana es mayor" and "Mi hermano es mayor" use the same form. They only change for number: mejores, peores, mayores, menores. "Mis abuelos son mayores que mis padres."
The common mistake is "más mejor." Mejor already means more good, so adding más doubles it. Also, más grande and más pequeño are fine for physical size; mayor and menor are best for age.

words.d: better — Mi dibujo es mejor que el tuyo; plural mejores
worse — El tráfico hoy es peor que ayer
older (for age) — Soy mayor que mi hermano
younger (for age) — Mi prima es menor que yo

look.title: Ages in One Family (Example)
look.prompt: Write three comparisons with mayor que or menor que. How many years older is Elena than Tomás?

check.q: Which sentence says My brother is older than I am?
choices: Mi hermano es más mayor que yo.
Mi hermano es menor que yo.
Mi hermano es mayora que yo.
Mi hermano es mayor que yo.
check.why: Older is mayor; más is not added, and mayor does not change for gender.

check.q: Choose the correct word: Esta película es ___ que la otra (better).
check.why: Mejor already means better; no más is needed.

check.q: What does Mis primos son menores que yo mean?
choices: My cousins are older than I am.
My cousins are younger than I am.
My cousins are smaller than I am.
My cousins are worse than I am.
check.why: Menor means younger; menores is the plural.

lessons.title: Describing a Famous Person
lessons.mainIdea: Describe a famous person with facts you know are true: identity, origin, traits and a comparison.
reading: Pick someone many people know, like the Mexican painter Frida Kahlo. Start with identity and origin, using ser: "Frida Kahlo es una pintora mexicana muy famosa" (Frida Kahlo is a very famous Mexican painter). Notice that pintora and mexicana both end in -a.

Add what she is known for, using only facts you are sure of: "Es famosa por sus autorretratos" (She is famous for her self-portraits). Chicago also has the National Museum of Mexican Art in Pilsen, a good place to see Mexican art up close.
You can also describe a sports star or singer. Use adjectives for traits you can see in their work: talentoso (talented), valiente (brave), creativo (creative). "Es muy talentosa y trabajadora."

End with a comparison for your opinion: "Para mí, su arte es más interesante que muchos otros." Words like para mí (for me) show it is your view, not a fact. Good descriptions separate facts from opinions.

words.d: painter (female) — el pintor for a male painter
famous — Frida Kahlo es famosa
talented — Es un cantante muy talentoso

look.title: Facts or Opinions?
look.text: 1. Frida Kahlo es de México. 2. Es una pintora famosa. 3. Para mí, es la mejor pintora del mundo. 4. Sus cuadros son muy coloridos. 5. Es más interesante que otros pintores. (1. Frida Kahlo is from Mexico. 2. She is a famous painter. 3. For me, she is the best painter in the world. 4. Her paintings are very colorful. 5. She is more interesting than other painters.)
look.prompt: Which sentences are facts and which are opinions? Write four sentences about a famous person you admire, with one comparison.

check.q: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Frida Kahlo es una pintora mexicano.
Frida Kahlo está una pintora mexicana.
Frida Kahlo es una pintora mexicana.
Frida Kahlo es una mexicana pintora.
check.why: Identity uses ser; mexicana goes after the noun and matches pintora.

check.q: Which phrase marks an opinion?
check.why: Para mí (for me) shows the statement is the writer's view.

check.q: Choose the adjective: Los cantantes son muy ___.
check.why: Cantantes here is masculine plural (los), so talentosos.

review.why: Casas is feminine plural, so blancas.

review.q: Which adjective has the same form for masculine and feminine?
review.why: Adjectives ending in -e, like amable, do not change for gender.

review.q: Which phrase says a good day?
review.why: Bueno shortens to buen before a masculine singular noun; día is masculine.

review.q: Which sentence says She has green eyes?
review.why: Tener for eyes; verdes matches ojos, which is masculine plural.

review.q: In the story, why does Gabriel change perro perdido?
choices: Canela is female, so it should be perra perdida.
Perro is not a Spanish word.
review.why: Nouns and adjectives change to match a female animal: perra perdida.

review.q: Which sentence says My sister is younger than I am?
choices: Mi hermana es más menor que yo.
Mi hermana es mayor que yo.
Mi hermana es menor que yo.
Mi hermana es menora que yo.
review.why: Younger is menor, with no más and no gender change.

review.q: What does Es un gran amigo mean?
choices: He is a physically big friend.
review.why: Gran before a noun means great.

choices: Mi perro es más grande que tu gato.
Mi perro es más grande de tu gato.
Mi perro es más grande como tu gato.
Mi perro es grande más que tu gato.
